analysis.one_liner: Lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission set safety standards for firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, vote, or cosponsor and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal consumer product safety law currently carves out pistols, revolvers, and other firearms from the definition of a consumer product, which means the Consumer Product Safety Commission cannot regulate them for safety. This bill would strike that carve-out, letting the Commission issue safety standards for guns and gun components just as it does for other household products. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who own, handle, or live around guns, since a safety agency could require design standards, issue recalls, and investigate defects the same way it does for cars' cribs, and power tools. Families of shooting victims injured by malfunctioning or defectively designed firearms could also benefit from fewer defective weapons on the market.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exclusion of pistols, revolvers, and other firearms from the Consumer Product Safety Act's definition of a consumer product, giving the Commission authority over them. [S3]

Also strikes the parallel rulemaking carve-out added by the 1976 Consumer Product Safety Commission Improvements Act, so the Commission could set safety standards for firearms and firearm components. [S2] [S3]
Firearms are currently the only widely sold consumer product exempt from federal product safety oversight, meaning no federal agency can order a recall of a defective gun. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and importers, who would face product safety standards, potential recalls, and defect liability for the first time. Some gun owners could also pay somewhat more if design changes raise manufacturing costs.

drawbacks.text: CPSC safety standards could raise the price of guns for buyers, and critics note the agency's process can be slow and heavy-handed for products some consider constitutionally protected. [S3]
Opponents argue product safety is a backdoor to gun control and that existing ATF regulation already covers firearms; the bill drew no cosponsors, including from other Democrats. [S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a straightforward one: a federal agency with recall and standards authority over defective products would apply to guns as it does to nearly everything else sold to consumers. The cost is higher prices for some guns and a genuinely contested legal question about applying a consumer agency to a product with special constitutional status. The design is simple and targeted, but with zero cosponsors it had no realistic path, so its merits were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Consumer Protection subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on June 17, 2021. [S1] [S5]
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day. [S5]
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce. [S5]
No member of the House, including fellow Democrats, signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]
No further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023, leaving the firearms exemption in place. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers keep their exemption from federal product safety standards, and no defective-gun recall authority exists. Gun owners see no change in price or design rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearm makers keep their regulatory exemption

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the committee she serves on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote in 18 months.

against.name: Firearm manufacturers and gun-rights groups
against.role: Industry and advocacy opponents of CPSC jurisdiction over firearms
against.what_they_did: Long opposed subjecting firearms to consumer product safety regulation, treating it as a step toward gun control; no member cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill and zero cosponsors joined from either party, so it never drew even same-party support.

industries.note: Guns are currently exempt from the Consumer Product Safety Act, so no federal agency can set design standards or order a recall of a defective gun. The bill would end that exemption, exposing manufacturers to safety standards and recalls; the exemption's benefit of keeping product-liability-style oversight off guns comes at the cost of consumers harmed by defective weapons.

Dealers could be required to pull defective models from shelves under Commission recall orders and could face inventory losses, while consumers would gain the same recall protections that apply to other products they buy.
